pages.title: What this unit is about
pages.body:
> 🌐 **Strand 3 — Communication Networks**
Sub-strand 3: Information Security

Staying safe online means understanding the threats people pose to each other, from cyberbullying and stalking to the techniques hackers use to steal information. In this unit you will learn to recognise these threats and protect yourself.

pages.title: Content standard and lessons
pages.body:
> 🎯 **Content standard**
- **B9.3.3.1** Recognise data threats and the means of protection.

> 🧭 **What you will be able to do**
- **B9.3.3.1.1** Discuss cyberbullying, cyberstalking, digital footprint and digital shadow on the Internet.
- **B9.3.3.1.2** Explain ten (10) information hacking techniques on the Internet environment.

> 🗺️ **Lessons in this unit**
- 10.1 Cyberbullying, Cyberstalking, Digital Footprint and Digital Shadow
- 10.2 Ten Information Hacking Techniques

**Core competencies developed:** Digital Literacy (DL6.1, DL5.1), Critical Thinking (CP6.4), Communication and Collaboration (CC8.5).

pages.title: Cyberbullying, Cyberstalking, Digital Footprint and Digital Shadow
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B9.3.3.1.1
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- discuss the nature of each;
- identify examples;
- discuss the effects of cyberbullying on individuals.
| **Term** | **Nature** | **Examples** |
|---|---|---|
| Cyberbullying | Using digital technology to **repeatedly** harass, threaten, embarrass or target another person | Insulting comments; spreading rumours; sharing embarrassing photos; excluding someone from a group chat; creating fake profiles to mock someone |
| Cyberstalking | Using the Internet to **persistently follow, monitor, threaten or contact** someone so that they feel afraid | Repeated unwanted messages; tracking someone’s location; monitoring all their posts; threatening emails |
| Digital footprint | The **trail of data you create** when you use the Internet (active footprint), plus data collected as you browse (passive) | Posts, comments, likes, photos you upload, online forms, search history |
| Digital shadow | Information about you that is **created or collected by others**, often without your knowledge; it can be larger than your own footprint | Photos others tag you in; CCTV; data held by apps, banks and schools; advertisers’ tracking cookies |
[[fig:c9-f12|Figure 11: Digital footprint and digital shadow]]
## Effects of cyberbullying on individuals
- **Emotional:** fear, sadness, anger, low self-esteem, anxiety and depression.
- **Academic:** loss of concentration, falling grades, avoiding school.
- **Social:** withdrawal from friends and family; loss of trust.
- **Physical:** headaches, sleep problems, poor appetite.
- **Serious harm:** in extreme cases, self-harm. Anyone affected should talk to a trusted adult, a teacher, a counsellor or a helpline immediately.

pages.title: Cyberbullying, Cyberstalking, Digital Footprint and Digital Shadow (continued)
pages.body:
> 🇬🇭 **Ghana connection — The law** Ghana’s **Cybersecurity Act, 2020 (Act 1038)** makes cyberstalking, sexual extortion and the non-consensual sharing of intimate images serious crimes, and the **Cybersecurity (Amendment) Bill, 2025** proposes stronger provisions on cyberbullying and online harassment. Report incidents to the **Cyber Security Authority** (call or text **292**, WhatsApp **0501603111**) or the police.
> 🧪 **Activity**
Watch a short film or read a story about cyberbullying. In groups, identify the bully, the victim and the bystanders; describe the effects on the victim; and role-play what an “upstander” (a bystander who helps) should do.

lessons.title: Ten Information Hacking Techniques

pages.title: Ten Information Hacking Techniques
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B9.3.3.1.2
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- brainstorm hacking techniques;
- explain ten hacking techniques and how to protect against them.
**Hacking** is gaining unauthorised access to computers, networks or data. The table explains ten common techniques that criminal hackers use.

pages.title: Ten Information Hacking Techniques (continued)
pages.body:
| **No.** | **Technique** | **How it works** | **Protection** |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Phishing | Fake emails, SMS (smishing), calls (vishing) or websites pretend to be a trusted organisation to trick you into revealing passwords, PINs or card details | Check sender and links; never share OTPs/PINs; type website addresses yourself |
| 2 | Keyloggers | Hidden software or devices record every key you press, capturing passwords | Antivirus; avoid public computers for banking; use 2FA |
| 3 | Denial of Service (DoS/DDoS) | Floods a website or server with fake traffic (often from thousands of infected devices, a **botnet**) so real users cannot access it | Firewalls, traffic filtering, DDoS-protection services |
| 4 | Eavesdropping / Man-in-the-middle | The attacker secretly intercepts communication, e.g. on unsecured public Wi-Fi, to read or alter it | HTTPS, VPN, avoid sensitive tasks on public Wi-Fi |
| 5 | Fake Wi-Fi access point (“evil twin”) | A hacker sets up a free Wi-Fi hotspot with a trustworthy-sounding name to capture users’ data | Use known networks; confirm the hotspot name with staff |
| 6 | Malware: viruses, worms and Trojans | Harmful programs hidden in downloads, attachments or pirated software damage files or open a “back door” | Antivirus; download from official sources; don’t open unknown attachments |
| 7 | Ransomware | Malware that encrypts your files and demands payment to unlock them | Regular offline/cloud backups; updates; antivirus |
| 8 | Password attacks (brute force, dictionary, credential stuffing) | Programs try millions of passwords, common words, or passwords leaked from other sites | Long, unique passphrases; password manager; 2FA; account lockout |
| 9 | Clickjacking | Invisible buttons or links are hidden over a web page so that you click something different from what you see | Updated browsers; avoid suspicious sites; don’t click unexpected pop-ups |
| 10 | Cookie theft / session hijacking | The attacker steals the browser cookie that keeps you logged in and uses it to access your account | Log out of shared computers; HTTPS sites; clear cookies |

pages.title: Ten Information Hacking Techniques (continued)
pages.body:
> ✨ **Did you know? — More techniques** Other common techniques include **social engineering** (manipulating people into breaking security rules), **SIM-swap fraud** (tricking a network into moving your number to the criminal’s SIM to receive your OTPs), **SQL injection** (inserting malicious code into website forms) and **shoulder surfing** (watching someone type a PIN).
> 🎯 **BECE focus — The strongest defences** **Strong unique passwords + two-factor authentication + software updates + antivirus + backups + thinking before you click.**
> 💡 **Career Corner** **Ethical hackers** (penetration testers) are hired by organisations to find weaknesses before criminals do. Cybersecurity is one of the fastest-growing career fields in Ghana and worldwide.
